summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp Python web application end-to-end: the DAO layer (SQL), views/routes (HTTP handlers and authorization), auth/session utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 configuration and templates, service setup, config and SQL migrations. The app is intentionally vulnerable and the code confirms this: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create, stored XSS enabled by globally disabled template autoescaping, unsalted MD5 password hashing, disabled CSRF protection, session cookies without HttpOnly, and missing authorization on all state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical (remote, unauthenticated code/data compromise is reachable).

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via student name
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-string formatting instead of a parameterized query, interpolating the attacker-controlled student name directly into SQL. The name comes from request.post()['name'] in the students view (sqli/views.py:57), which handles POST /students/ with no authentication decorator, so any anonymous visitor can inject. A payload such as x'); DROP TABLE marks; -- or a stacked/sub-query can read or destroy arbitrary data in the PostgreSQL database. This is the only query in the codebase that is not parameterized; all other DAO methods use placeholders correctly.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q)  <- name flows from views.students POST handler: data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name']) (sqli/views.py:54-57). No @authorize on the route (sqli/routes.py:14).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/f-strings/concatenation from request data.

findings.title: Stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False in Jinja2 setup
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered verbatim, producing stored/reflected XSS. Concretely, course review text is written by any anonymous user (POST /courses/{id}/review, sqli/views.py:129) with no sanitization and later rendered raw at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22, and student names are rendered raw at sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16 (names are also the SQLi sink). An attacker can submit <script>...</script> that executes in every visitor's browser, including admins, enabling session/credential theft (worsened by HttpOnly being off).
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False) (sqli/app.py:35). Sinks: {{ review.review_text }} (course.jinja2:22), {{ name }} (students.jinja2:16), {{ course.description }} (course.jinja2:15). Source: Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from request.post() (views.py:120-129).
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (remove autoescape=False / set autoescape=True) and only mark explicitly-trusted values as safe. Validate/escape review and name input at the boundary.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing and verification
findings.description: Passwords are stored and verified as unsalted MD5 hashes. MD5 is extremely fast and broken for this purpose; combined with no per-user salt, stored hashes (e.g. exfiltrated via the SQL injection above) are trivially reversed with rainbow tables or brute force. The seed data confirms the scheme (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 uses md5('superadmin') etc.). The comparison also uses a non-constant-time == on the hex digest (minor timing leak).
findings.evidence: from hashlib import md5 (user.py:1); return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() (user.py:41). Hashes seeded with SQL md5() in migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13.
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted KDF such as argon2id or bcrypt (e.g. passlib/argon2-cffi), migrate stored hashes, and compare using the library's verify (constant-time).

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware defined but not enabled
findings.description: A working CSRF-validation middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates render a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no POST request's token is ever checked. All state-changing endpoints (login at POST /, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate marks, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker page can force an authenticated admin's browser to create records, assign marks, or log out.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] (sqli/app.py:25-29); the csrf_middleware that pops/validates session['_csrf_token'] vs formdata is fully implemented at sqli/middlewares.py:25-38 but never registered.
findings.recommendation: Register csrf_middleware in the middlewares list (and import it) so token validation runs on every POST; reject requests with missing/mismatched tokens.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, student/course/review creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students with no authentication or admin check — it is only gated in the UI by a template condition (course.jinja2:41 {% if auth_user.is_admin %}), which an attacker simply ignores by POSTing directly to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to the other mutating handlers: students POST (views.py:51-60, also the SQLi sink), courses POST (views.py:83-93), and review POST (views.py:111-131) — none use the @authorize decorator that is available in sqli/utils/auth.py. Only logout is protected. Any anonymous user can create students/courses, post reviews, and grade students.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) with no @authorize/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) (views.py:134-152). Route registered without protection (routes.py:21-23). Decorator authorize(ensure_admin=...) exists at utils/auth.py:12-23 but is only applied to logout.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize() / @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to all mutating handlers (evaluate as admin-only; student/course/review creation as at least authenticated), enforcing authorization server-side rather than in templates.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS reachable in this app (autoescape disabled, unauthenticated review posting), an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier to hijack authenticated/admin sessions. The cookie is also not marked Secure, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use the default httponly=True, add secure=True (serve over HTTPS), and set samesite='Lax'/'Strict' on the session storage.

findings.title: Application runs with debug=True exposing internals
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is instantiated with debug=True. In debug mode aiohttp performs extra checks and can surface more verbose diagnostics; combined with logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) in run.py:11, this increases the chance of leaking internal state and stack details to logs/responses and should not be used in production.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug and log level from environment/config and default to debug=False with INFO/WARNING logging in production.
